title: The Woman and Her Bear Foster-Son
subtitle: An animal becomes part of a household

learningObjectives.text: What does the old woman feed the bear cub?
What does the old woman tell the bear to remember when playing with children?

bear.author: Greenlandic storytellers, collected by Knud Rasmussen
bear.locator: The Woman Who Had A Bear As A Foster-Son; The Woman Who Had A Bear As A Foster-Son, normalized characters 394-1594
bear.excerpt: The old woman received a piece from the ribs as her share, and took it home to her house. After she had come home to her house, the wife of the man who had killed the bear came to the window and said: "Dear little old woman in there, would you like to have a bear's cub?" And the old woman went and fetched it, and brought it into her house, shifted her lamp, and placed the cub, because it was frozen, up on to the drying frame to thaw. Suddenly she noticed that it moved a little, and took it down to warm it. Then she roasted some blubber, for she had heard that bears lived on blubber, and in this way she fed it from that time onwards, giving it greaves to eat and melted blubber to drink, and it lay beside her at night. And after it had begun to lie beside her at night it grew very fast, and she began to talk to it in human speech, and thus it gained the mind of a human being, and when it wished to ask its foster-mother for food, it would sniff. The old woman now no longer suffered want, and those living near brought her food for the cub. The children came sometimes to play with it, but then the old woman would say: "Little bear, remember to sheathe your claws when you play with them.
bear.note: Verbatim English rendering by Worster from stories collected by Rasmussen in Greenland. The book title uses an outdated ethnonym; this lesson identifies the collection's Greenland scope.

narrativeBlocks.title: A cub comes into the house
narrativeBlocks.body: A hunter's household gives an old woman a bear cub. She warms it beside her lamp and feeds it blubber.

narrativeBlocks.title: The cub learns restraint
narrativeBlocks.body: The story says the bear grows quickly and joins the children at play. The old woman reminds it to sheath its claws.

narrativeBlocks.title: One named Greenland tale
narrativeBlocks.body: This passage comes from Rasmussen's collection and Worster's English version. Do not turn this single narrative into a universal statement about Inuit relationships with bears.

narrativeBlocks.title: Kinship across species in this story
narrativeBlocks.body: The title calls the animal a foster-son; the narrative focuses on care, food, and limits during play.
